title: My Game is Ready and I Signed Up for a Steam Dev Account Only to Wait 2 Months - What Do I Do?
author: OriginlessGamer
selftext:
Hello sloppers, I mean, vibecoders, so... 

It took me \~10 days to AI slop a game, and it's mostly ready (I really tried). 

ChatGPT = $20 (main code bro + art)  
Gemini = $5 (helper code bro)  
ElevenLabs = $6 (voiceover)  
Suno AI = $10 (music)  
Steamworks = $100 (come on man)

So, the tools cost me $41 and the Steam account is $100

I have a bunch of time till it all comes together (if ever), what would you spend this time on?

Would you build features, marketing, videos, description, discount table, or something else like that - maybe even another game?

TLDR; my game is ready, my Steam account is pending, I have 2 months of wait time, and zero ideas

comments.author: Sufficient_Crew_5321
comments.body: I would use those two months as preparation time rather than thinking of it as a delay. This is a good opportunity to improve screenshots, create a trailer, test the game with new players, gather feedback, fix bugs, and start building a small community around the project. You can also work on your Steam store page and collect wishlists before launch. Many developers end up wishing they had more time to prepare, so using this period effectively could make a big difference when the game finally goes live.

replies.author: OriginlessGamer
replies.body: thanks! I think I might be underestimating all this pre-launch work, so I should definitely give it more attention

replies.author: Sufficient_Crew_5321
replies.body: Absolutely. A lot of developers focus entirely on finishing the game and then realize the launch itself is almost a separate project. Things like store page optimization, trailers, screenshots, onboarding, community building, and bug fixing can have a huge impact on how the game performs after release. Having extra time to polish those areas can be a real advantage.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Either you are a savant or that's a lot of waiting just to be disappointed.

I assure you, if you only spent 10 days on your game, and you yourself call it slop, once it does hit steam we are likely to see a post back here asking why no one is playing the game and "Why is marketing so hard?"

It's great to finish something and put yourself out there, but we're in an era where quality is the only way to differentiate yourself or your product amongst a sea of slop. Even if you spend the next two months diligently polishing whatever you have, it's still going to be a hard sell to compete for buyers' attention.
